takeaway: Pyloric stenosis: a young boy with non-bilious projectile vomiting and an olive-sized mass in the right upper quadrant, from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.

question.text: A 7-week-old boy has non-bilious vomiting and dehydration. An olive-sized mass is felt in the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis?
question.say: A seven-week-old boy presents with non-bilious vomiting and dehydration. On examination there is an olive-sized mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis?

lines.text: A 7-week-old boy shoots out non-bilious projectile vomit.
lines.say: This seven-week-old boy has non-bilious, projectile vomiting, and he is getting dehydrated.

lines.text: An olive-sized mass in the right upper quadrant.
lines.say: The doctor feels an olive-sized mass in the right upper quadrant. Here it is, a grumpy little olive.

lines.text: The thick pylorus muscle blocks the stomach exit.
lines.say: (laugh) And the angry bodybuilder next to it is the thick pylorus muscle, blocking the stomach exit.

lines.text: In hypertrophic pyloric stenosis the pyloric muscle is overgrown.
lines.say: In hypertrophic pyloric stenosis the pyloric lumen is obstructed by muscular hypertrophy.

lines.text: It most commonly affects males in the first few months of life.
lines.say: It most commonly affects males in the first few months of life.

lines.text: Remember: projectile non-bilious vomiting with an olive-sized mass is pyloric stenosis.
lines.say: Remember: projectile non-bilious vomiting with an olive-sized mass means pyloric stenosis.
